lead: The 8253 and 8254 are programmable interval timers. Each chip holds three independent 16-bit down counters. You load a count, a clock drives the counter down, and an OUT pin changes state at terminal count. One chip turns a fixed clock into delays, pulse trains and square waves while the CPU does other work. It appears on 8085 and 8086 boards and in motor pulse generation. Only a few universities teach this chapter.
prereq: You need: delay loops from Unit 3 and 8051 timer programming from Unit 4 for comparison.

sections.h3: Three counters and one control word

blocks.text: Each chip has three independent 16-bit down counters, numbered 0, 1 and 2. Every counter has a CLK input, a GATE input and an OUT pin. The clock drives the counter down by one on each falling edge. GATE enables or triggers counting, depending on the mode. OUT changes state at terminal count. The CPU programs the count once and continues.

One control word selects the counter and its behaviour. SC1 SC0 choose counter 0, 1 or 2. RW1 RW0 choose LSB only, MSB only, or LSB then MSB. M2 M1 M0 choose one of six modes. The BCD bit chooses binary or binary-coded decimal counting. A loaded count of 0 means 65536 in binary mode and 10000 in BCD mode. The count is:

blocks.where: N is the loaded count; f_clk is the clock frequency in hertz; T_delay is the wanted delay in seconds.

blocks.text: The figure uses small counts: mode 2 with count 3 and mode 3 with count 4.

sections.h3: The six modes in one line each

blocks.text: The six modes decide what OUT does. Mode 2 is a rate generator: OUT stays high, goes low for one clock at terminal count, then reloads. Mode 3 makes a square wave: OUT is high for half the count and low for half the count; with an odd count the high time is one clock longer than the low time. The table gives each mode in one line.

blocks.text: GATE matters. In mode 1 and mode 5 a rising edge on GATE starts the pulse. In mode 2 and mode 3 GATE low stops the counter; GATE high lets it run. In mode 0 and mode 4 GATE low stops counting and GATE high resumes. Check the mode before you connect a gate signal.

Reading a running counter is unsafe. The low byte and high byte can come from two different counts. The latch command solves this. Write a control word with RW1 RW0 = 00 and the counter's SC bits; the chip copies the current count into a latch. Read the low byte, then the high byte. The latch holds one value.

The 8254 adds a read-back command and a status byte. The 8253 does not have them. The status byte shows the OUT pin state, the NULL COUNT flag (0 = a count has been loaded into the counting element, 1 = it has not), the RW1 RW0 bits, the mode bits and the BCD bit. If a question says 8254 read-back, do not apply it to the 8253.

Write the control word first, then the count bytes in the order fixed by RW1 RW0. For LSB-then-MSB, write low byte then high byte. Writing high byte first loads a wrong number, and the error appears only when you measure timing. Use the latch before any two-byte read of a running counter.

figure.caption: Mode 2 with count 3 makes OUT low for one clock in every three; mode 3 with count 4 makes a square wave of period four clocks.

examples.question: A 1 MHz clock drives counter 0. Produce an OUT0 pulse train of period 1 ms (1 kHz) using mode 2, binary, LSB first. Give the control word and the bytes written.
steps: Write 34H to control, E8H to counter 0, then 03H.
OUT0 is a 1 kHz pulse train; terminal count repeats every 1 ms.
examples.answer: Control word 34H; count 1000 (03E8H); OUT0 is 1 kHz; write E8H then 03H to counter 0.
examples.check:
f_clk = 1_000_000
t_delay = 1e-3
count = int(t_delay / (1 / f_clk))
cw = (0 << 6) | (3 << 4) | (2 << 1) | 0
f_out = f_clk / count
print(count)
print(cw)
print(f_out)

traps: Writing the high byte first when the control word asks for LSB first loads a wrong count; you see it only when timing is measured.
Reading a running counter without the latch mixes low and high bytes from two different counts.
Loading 0 does not stop a counter; it loads 65536 in binary mode and 10000 in BCD mode.
Mode 2 repeats; it is a rate generator, not a one-shot delay. Mode 3 is the square wave.
The 8253 has no read-back command or status byte; those belong to the 8254.

quiz.q: How many counters does an 8253 have, and how wide is each?
Why does a loaded count of 0 mean 65536?
quiz.a: A 16-bit counter counts 0 to 65535; 0 is decoded as the full terminal count.

quiz.q: A 2 MHz clock feeds mode 2 with count 2000. Find the OUT frequency.

quiz.a: SC=01 counter 1; RW=11 LSB then MSB; M=011 mode 3; BCD=0 binary.

quiz.q: Why latch a counter before reading it while it runs?
quiz.a: So low and high bytes come from the same count.

quiz.q: Mode 2 has count 3 and a 1 MHz clock. Describe OUT.
quiz.a: OUT is high for two clocks, low for one clock, repeating every 3 µs; pulse frequency is 333.3 kHz.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern microcontrollers keep this idea inside timer/counter blocks with prescalers, compare registers and PWM outputs. The 8254 read-back command survives in compatibility chips and teaching boards. Search for '8254 read-back command', 'timer prescaler' and 'PWM timer' to go further.
